key_features.classic_presentation: Biliary colic presents with episodic RUQ or epigastric pain triggered by fatty meals. Pain builds to peak over 15 minutes, plateaus for 1-4 hours, then gradually resolves. No fever. Recurrent episodes over weeks to months.
key_features.typical_demographics: Same as cholecystitis - Female, Forty, Fat, Fertile. 10-15% of US adults have gallstones.
key_features.pathophysiology_brief: Temporary cystic duct obstruction by gallstone causes gallbladder spasm and pain. Stone passes, pain resolves. No inflammation.

diagnostic_questions.context: Intermittent pattern distinguishes from cholecystitis. Each episode lasts 30min-6h (typically 1-4h).
RUQ or epigastric. May radiate to right scapula.
Often triggered by fatty meals (causes CCK release → gallbladder contraction).
NO fever in uncomplicated biliary colic. Fever indicates cholecystitis.
Recurrent episodes over weeks to months is typical. Single first episode is less specific.
Individual episodes last 1-6 hours. If >6 hours consider cholecystitis.

differential_diagnosis.key_difference: Constant pain >6 hours, fever, more severe

red_flags.action: Possible progression to cholecystitis - ER evaluation
Cholecystitis, not simple colic - urgent care needed

typical_management: Pain control during episodes. Elective cholecystectomy to prevent recurrence and complications. Most progress to cholecystitis within 2-3 years if not treated.
disposition: Outpatient management if uncomplicated. Surgical referral for cholecystectomy.
patient_education: Biliary colic is pain from gallstones temporarily blocking the gallbladder duct. While not immediately dangerous, it often recurs and can progress to gallbladder inflammation. Gallbladder removal is the definitive treatment.
